title: Beautiful Array
description: Brute force to optimized: searching over permutations versus a direct parity-based recursive construction guaranteed correct by a mathematical invariant.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer n, construct a "beautiful array": a permutation of the integers from 1 to n such that for every pair of indices i < k < j, arr[k] times 2 is never equal to arr[i] plus arr[j] (equivalently, arr[k] is never the exact average of some earlier and later element). Any valid beautiful array may be returned.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"No element is the exact average of an earlier and later element\"","A parity trick: splitting values into all-odd and all-even groups guarantees this automatically"],["A recursive-feeling structure (works for n, should work for smaller n too)","Divide and conquer: build smaller beautiful arrays and combine them via a value transformation"]]}

blocks.text: If arr[k] were exactly the average of arr[i] and arr[j] (with i before k before j), then arr[i] + arr[j] must equal 2 times arr[k], meaning arr[i] and arr[j] must have the SAME parity (both odd or both even) for their sum to be even, matching 2*arr[k]. This is the key structural fact that a parity-based split exploits.

blocks.title: Analogy: Separating Left- and Right-Handed Guests to Avoid an Awkward Average
blocks.text: Picture wanting to seat guests so no guest's "handedness score" is ever exactly the midpoint of two others around them. If left-handed guests (odd scores) are grouped entirely separately from right-handed guests (even scores) in the seating order, an odd-scored guest can never be exactly the midpoint of two even-scored guests (or vice versa), since odd and even numbers can never average to each other's type cleanly across the two groups.

blocks.caption: Since only same-parity pairs can average to an integer matching another same-parity value, splitting into odd/even groups helps enforce the beautiful condition

blocks.text: Result: [1, 3, 2, 4], one valid beautiful array. No arr[k] is ever the exact average of an earlier and later element.

Before trying to construct or verify permutations directly, notice that if the ENTIRE left portion of the array uses only odd values and the entire right portion uses only even values (or vice versa), no element from one portion can ever be the average of two elements straddling it from different portions, since odd and even values cannot average to an integer of the other type in the way required. Applying this same idea recursively WITHIN each portion builds the full array.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If arr[i] and arr[j] have DIFFERENT parity, their sum is odd, so 2*arr[k] (always even) can never equal it, meaning the beautiful condition is automatically satisfied whenever i and j fall on opposite sides of a odd/even split boundary at k.

Observation 2: This means a beautiful array can be built by placing ALL values that map to one parity group in one contiguous block, and all values mapping to the other parity group in another contiguous block, since no problematic triple can span the boundary between them.

Observation 3: WITHIN each block, the same "no element is the average of two others" property still needs to hold, but this is exactly the same original problem at a smaller size, just with the values remapped (a beautiful array of size m mapped to "2x-1" for all-odd values 1,3,5,... or "2x" for all-even values 2,4,6,...).

Observation 4: This gives a clean recursive construction: build a smaller beautiful array for the left half's size, map it to odd values; build a smaller beautiful array for the right half's size, map it to even values; concatenate them.

This leads to recursively building beautiful arrays for smaller sizes, mapping one to all-odd values and the other to all-even values, and concatenating them, since this construction automatically satisfies the beautiful condition both within each half and across the odd/even boundary.
Generate permutations (or build greedily with backtracking) and check the beautiful condition directly by scanning all valid triples.

items: Generate a candidate permutation of 1 to n (via backtracking or brute enumeration).
For every triple i < k < j, check whether arr[k]*2 equals arr[i]+arr[j].
If any triple violates the condition, discard the candidate and try another.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Directly searching over permutations and validating each one against the definition is the most literal approach.
This is computationally infeasible for anything beyond very small n, since there are n-factorial permutations to potentially try.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: up to O(n! times n cubed) in the worst case, trying permutations and validating each with a triple-check.
Space: O(n) per candidate.
Limitation: completely infeasible for n up to 1000; the parity-based divide-and-conquer construction directly builds a valid beautiful array in O(n log n) without any trial and error.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why searching for a valid permutation is unnecessary: a DIRECT construction exists, based purely on parity, that is guaranteed correct by mathematical argument rather than trial and error.

The recursive construction: beautifulArray(1) = [1] (trivially beautiful). For n > 1, recursively build a beautiful array for ceil(n/2), map each value x to 2x-1 (giving all odd values), and a beautiful array for floor(n/2), map each value x to 2x (giving all even values); concatenate the odd-mapped array followed by the even-mapped array.

Why the mapping preserves beauty WITHIN each half: since x -> 2x-1 and x -> 2x are both strictly increasing linear transformations, if the ORIGINAL smaller beautiful array had no element that was the average of two others, applying this same linear transform to every element preserves that property exactly (linear transforms preserve average relationships).

Why concatenation is safe ACROSS the two halves: any triple spanning both halves has its i and j values in different parity groups (or arr[k] in one group and arr[i],arr[j] split across groups), and the earlier parity argument guarantees no such triple can satisfy the beautiful-breaking equation.

The core idea: recursively construct smaller beautiful arrays, remap them to disjoint odd/even value ranges, and concatenate, using memoization to avoid recomputation for repeated subproblem sizes.

Recursively build: base case n=1 returns [1]. Otherwise, build a beautiful array of size ceil(n/2), map each value x to 2x-1; build a beautiful array of size floor(n/2), map each value x to 2x; concatenate the two mapped arrays, memoizing by size to avoid recomputation.

blocks.caption: Recursively build smaller beautiful arrays, remap to odd/even ranges, concatenate

blocks.text: Linear transformations (x -> 2x-1 for odd, x -> 2x for even) preserve the "no element is the average of two others" property exactly, since if a smaller array had no such violating triple, scaling and shifting every element the same way cannot introduce one (averages scale and shift consistently). Concatenating an all-odd block with an all-even block introduces no NEW violations across the boundary, because any candidate arr[k] average requires arr[i] and arr[j] to share the same parity as each other (to sum to an even number matching 2*arr[k]), which is impossible for i, j straddling the odd/even boundary in opposite blocks. This recursive construction is therefore guaranteed correct at every level.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), each recursive level processes O(n) total elements across O(log n) levels.
Space: O(n log n) without memoization sharing, O(n) with memoization avoiding duplicate subproblem storage for repeated sizes.

blocks.text: Beautiful Array is a striking example of a "construct directly using a mathematical invariant" divide-and-conquer problem, where parity (odd versus even) is the key structural property that makes a direct, verification-free construction possible.

items: Mapping to 2x and 2x-1 inconsistently between the two halves, breaking the guarantee that the two blocks occupy fully disjoint odd/even ranges.
Forgetting to use ceil for one half's size and floor for the other, causing an incorrect total count of elements (must sum to exactly n).

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the key parity fact, "odd + odd and even + even are even, but odd + even is odd, so 2*arr[k] can never match a straddling pair of opposite parity," demonstrates the mathematical insight driving the entire construction.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "construct an array avoiding an average-based condition", think: parity split, odd values in one contiguous block, even values in another, recursively.

items: How would you prove formally that this construction always satisfies the beautiful condition for all n?
How would you adapt this idea to a different "no element is the weighted average" variant of the condition?
Any "construct directly using a mathematical invariant, avoid searching" divide-and-conquer problem.
Parity-based tricks appear broadly in combinatorial construction problems beyond this one.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The permutation-search approach is factorially infeasible; the parity-based recursive construction runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space, directly guaranteeing correctness.

items: Pattern: parity-based divide-and-conquer construction, exploiting that odd+odd and even+even sums are even, while odd+even sums are odd.
Core Idea: recursively build smaller beautiful arrays, map one to all-odd values (2x-1) and the other to all-even values (2x), concatenate.
Time: factorially infeasible for permutation search, O(n log n) for the constructive approach.
Space: O(n) for the constructive approach (with memoization).
Most Important Observation: linear odd/even remapping preserves the "no average" property both within each half and across their boundary.
Interview Difficulty: a clever, mathematically elegant divide-and-conquer construction problem.
One line memory trick: odd values on one side, even values on the other, built recursively.
